steps.prompt: Why does the speaker say a round box first, and the box after that?
options: The first time is new information; after that we both know which box.
Because the box is round and not square like the others.
Because the second sentence is longer than the first one.
steps.answer: The first time is new information; after that we both know which box.
steps.why: A / an introduces something new; the is for something we have already met or can both identify.

steps.title: a / an, the, and no article
steps.html:
ArticleUse it forExample
a / anone of many, first mentionIt’s a metal ball.
a / ana job or what something isShe’s an architect.
thewe both know which oneThe box does not close.
thethere is only onethe sun, the internet, the seafront
thewith a superlativeIt’s the heaviest of the five.
—things in general (plural)Possessions are about time.
—uncountable things in generalIt’s made of metal.

Use an before a vowel sound: an antique ring, an hour — but a university, because it begins with a /j/ sound.

Say the when the listener can already work out which one you mean — from the situation, or because you said it before.

Use no article for plural and uncountable nouns when you mean them in general: I like books. It’s made of leather.

The most common mistake is dropping a before a job: say She’s a nurse, not She’s nurse.

How much and how many of something — that is the next lesson.

steps.title: Five things, one person
steps.html:
A museum in my city asked people to do something strange: choose five objects from your home that would tell a stranger who you are. Not the most valuable five. The five that mean something. I thought it would take ten minutes. It took me a week.

The first was easy. A green bicycle. Not the green bicycle in the photograph on my wall — that one was stolen — but the plastic-and-metal one I bought to replace it. It is not fashionable and it is certainly not brand new. The condition is terrible. I have ridden it every day for nine years.

Then a leather notebook, heavy, with thin paper and a pale blue cover. I do not write in it. I collect train tickets in it, and the collection is now nearly full.

Then an antique wooden spoon that belonged to my grandmother. It is the only object in the house that is older than my father.

The fourth was a lamp — a shiny, bright, completely useless lamp that a friend gave me. My flat is minimalist because I cannot afford furniture, and the lamp is the one thing in it that argues with the walls.

The fifth took the rest of the week. In the end I chose a key. It opens a door in a city I no longer live in, and it is not suitable for anything now, but I have never been able to throw it away.

Here is what surprised me. Nothing on my list was expensive, and nothing was essential. Ask somebody what possessions they own and they will tell you about money. Ask them for five objects and they will tell you about their life.

Note. Written for this course as a reading text, in the first person. The museum project and the writer are invented; the idea — a personal collection chosen for meaning rather than value — is the one behind the time-capsule and ‘object stories’ projects that museums run. No words are attributed to a real person.
